# Async execution, waiting and failure

## Start with one representative question

[S01-Q024](#S01-Q024)

<p>How does async/await organize the execution of a C# operation that waits for I/O? Trace the caller before, during and after an awaited operation.</p>

## One group objective and observable capabilities

<p>Explain an asynchronous operation from invocation through waiting, completion and failure.</p>

<ul>
<li>Distinguish an operation’s completion contract from its execution resources.</li>
<li>Trace awaited I/O and where an error is observed.</li>
<li>Choose I/O concurrency or CPU parallelism from a workload budget.</li>
</ul>

**Prerequisites**

No catalog prerequisite. Establish the terms and scenario assumptions in the foundation questions before progressing; a published lesson is not evidence that you know them.

<p>First track the operation rather than imagining a dedicated thread. That trace explains waiting and exception observation, then gives a basis for deciding whether the workload needs asynchronous I/O or CPU parallelism.</p>

### S01-Q024 · Foundation

<p>How does async/await organize the execution of a C# operation that waits for I/O? Trace the caller before, during and after an awaited operation.</p>

**Source:** [S01-Q024](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q024)

<p class="scope-note">Version-sensitive scope: state the actual runtime/framework/provider and check official documentation before making technical claims. This question bank does not certify current behavior, product defaults or performance results.</p>

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S01-Q024](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q024)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> How does `async`/`await` work?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Explain the sequence of work and waiting before discussing implementation details. Keep an asynchronous operation separate from a claim about a dedicated thread.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Build a causal model of an awaited operation.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>State runtime and application context; consult official documentation before depending on continuation scheduling or context-capture behavior.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Traces completion, an already-completed operation and an actual asynchronous wait.</li>
<li>Distinguishes the operation’s result from how code resumes and proposes an observable check.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Saying async automatically creates a new thread or makes CPU computation faster.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>What changes in your trace if the awaited operation is already complete?</li>
</ul>

<a id="S01-Q025"></a>

### S01-Q025 · Foundation

<p>What is the difference between Task and Thread when designing a concurrent .NET operation? Explain what each represents before choosing one.</p>

**Source:** [S01-Q025](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q025)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S01-Q025](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q025)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> Compare `Task` and `Thread`.

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Compare a unit of work or completion contract with an execution resource. Use the workload to explain the decision rather than treating their names as equivalents.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Separate operation lifetime from execution-resource lifetime.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>State whether the work waits for I/O, consumes CPU or needs a dedicated execution resource; precise scheduling claims require the target runtime.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Explains completion, waiting and execution in one concrete example.</li>
<li>Justifies a choice and identifies the evidence needed for any throughput or resource claim.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Assuming every Task owns a thread for its whole lifetime.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>When would a dedicated thread be a consequential requirement rather than an implementation preference?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S01-Q026"></a>

### S01-Q026 · Mechanism

<p>How does asynchronous I/O differ from using a blocking thread to wait for I/O? Compare what happens while a request is waiting.</p>

**Source:** [S01-Q026](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q026)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S01-Q026](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q026)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> How does asynchronous I/O differ from traditional threading?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Follow the operation and execution resources through the waiting period. Keep I/O waiting separate from CPU work and from promises about faster individual requests.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Explain resource use during waiting and its relevance to concurrent load.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Use an API calling a slow external dependency; identify its actual async support and avoid assuming all wrappers provide asynchronous I/O.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Traces where work and waiting occur for the two approaches.</li>
<li>Relates the difference to capacity and proposes measurements under representative concurrency.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Calling Task.Run around a blocking operation equivalent to genuine asynchronous I/O.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>Which metrics would distinguish less blocking from a faster external dependency?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S01-Q030"></a>

### S01-Q030 · Failure cases

<p>How do exceptions reach the caller through asynchronous C# code? Trace an awaited failure and explain what you would examine when an operation is not awaited.</p>

**Source:** [S01-Q030](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q030)

<p class="scope-note">Version-sensitive scope: state the actual runtime/framework/provider and check official documentation before making technical claims. This question bank does not certify current behavior, product defaults or performance results.</p>

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S01-Q030](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q030)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> How do exceptions propagate through asynchronous code?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Identify where failure is represented and where it is observed. The goal is a clear error boundary, not merely adding a try/catch somewhere.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Predict failure observation across asynchronous call boundaries.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>State runtime, return type and calling context; check official documentation before asserting behavior for async void, task composition or unobserved failures.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Traces invocation, completion and the point where the caller can handle an error.</li>
<li>Includes a failure test and a deliberate strategy for reporting work outside the request lifetime.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Assuming a synchronous try/catch around invocation observes every later failure.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>What changes when several asynchronous operations are composed?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S01-Q031"></a>

### S01-Q031 · Trade-offs

<p>When should CPU-bound work use parallelism instead of being treated as asynchronous I/O? Explain how you would decide the amount of concurrency.</p>

**Source:** [S01-Q031](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q031)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S01-Q031](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q031)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> When should CPU-bound work use parallelism rather than asynchronous I/O?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Distinguish waiting for an external operation from doing computation. A choice must account for available capacity and the effect on other requests.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Choose concurrency from workload and resource constraints.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Use a hypothetical compute-heavy task in a service; state input size, CPU budget and competing workload before making performance claims.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Explains which work could run concurrently and what limits useful parallelism.</li>
<li>Proposes comparable measurements of throughput, latency and CPU use before increasing concurrency.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Assuming an async signature or more tasks automatically accelerates CPU work.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>How would your choice change when the service is already CPU-saturated?</li>
</ul>

</details>

## Combined production exercise — agent-added

<p>A hypothetical API downloads data and then performs a compute-heavy transformation. Trace success and a download failure, separate waiting from computation, and propose a concurrency limit. Identify the runtime/context assumptions to verify officially and measurements needed before promising higher capacity.</p>

## Short rubric — use only with an actual attempt

**Basic answer**

<p>Explains Task, Thread and await with a consistent operation trace.</p>

**Senior answer**

<p>Handles failure observation and workload-dependent concurrency while stating context and resource boundaries.</p>

**Still needs evidence**

<p>A fluent definition or an async method signature does not demonstrate resource behavior or improved throughput.</p>
